attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter, endorsed.

semantics.note: Keeps the bubble-implosion antecedent, the either-path scope and the 'I fear' qualifier. 'I fear' voices worry, not a firm commitment, like 'I suspect'. Under the policy that makes it a hedged claim that is not scored.

contract.note: The contract admits 'I fear' expresses uncertainty but still treats the claim as scorable on a plain reading. Policy says plain-reading scoring applies only to firm language. The 20,000 threshold is also the drafter's own reading. The antecedent is also unknown.

evidence.note: Block's own disclosure of a cut from about 10,000 to under 6,000 staff, framed as reorganizing around AI tools after a strong year. It is not a loss caused by a bubble implosion.

reviews.rationale: The claim is phrased as a fear ('I fear'), which is hedged language and is not scored. Even if it were firm, the conditional's antecedent is not established: nothing in the packet shows a broad AI bubble implosion. The Block layoffs are AI-linked restructuring, not losses caused by a collapse.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter, endorsed.

semantics.note: 'Is going to' and 'will' make this a firm forecast. 'At some point' gives no deadline. The normalization keeps both alternatives (price increases or onerous new rates) and the effect on enterprise customers.

contract.note: Reading the claim as the chain from provider costs to repricing to enterprise rejection is ordinary and fair. Breadth of rejection is undefined. The early-resolution rule needs the full chain documented.

evidence.note: April 2026 report: GitHub says it can no longer absorb rising inference costs and is moving to usage-based billing. This supports only the cost-pressure and repricing part.
GitHub's own changelog: usage-based billing took effect June 1, 2026. It confirms the repricing but not enterprise rejection.
Enterprises such as Microsoft, Accenture and Amazon curbed internal token spend. That is cost control over usage, not rejection of purchases because of provider price increases.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline. GitHub's cost-driven move to usage-based billing supports the repricing part. No evidence shows established enterprises rejecting or cutting back the affected purchases because the new prices could not be justified. The early-resolution rule is not met, so the claim stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own explanatory sentence, endorsed. The comparative premise rests on reports he cites from OpenAI.

semantics.note: 'This is because' explains the reported higher hallucination rate. The normalization states that premise as fact, which matches how Zitron uses it, though he based it on reports.

contract.note: It is fair to test the mechanism and the comparison against the September 2024 o1-preview. It is also fair to say that limited benchmarks cannot settle causation.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own o1-preview system card: its evals show o1-preview hallucinating less than GPT-4o, but it also notes anecdotal feedback the other way. The evals are limited and come from the company itself, so they challenge the premise without settling it.
OpenAI's launch post describes learned self-correction through RL. It does not identify a separate checking component or a cause of hallucinations.

reviews.rationale: No architecture documentation or controlled ablation isolates the 'work-checking' mechanism. The comparative premise is disputed: OpenAI's limited evals show fewer hallucinations, while anecdotal reports show more. The contract says a limited benchmark cannot settle the mechanism, so the evidence does not resolve the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter, endorsed.

semantics.note: 'I don't think it's going to be there' is an ordinary belief statement and counts as a firm forecast. But the normalization drops his qualifier that the contribution must be 'magnitudes higher' if capex rose. That overstates the claim as no material AI growth at all. The contract restores the qualifier.

contract.note: Limiting the window to Q1 2025 and the firms to the four named is a reasonable reading, and the contract keeps the capex qualifier. Materiality and the required ratio to capex are undefined, so the interpretation decides the result.

evidence.note: Microsoft's own disclosure for Jan–Mar 2025: Azure grew 33%, including 16 points from AI services. This is meaningful realized AI growth at one named firm, with no comparison to capex.

Microsoft's own disclosure for Oct–Dec 2024: AI infrastructure costs squeezed margins. The same page shows AI adding 13 points to Azure growth. This bears on the investment qualifier but does not settle it.

reviews.rationale: The window has passed. Microsoft reported meaningful realized AI contributions to Azure growth, which counts against the forecast for that firm. The packet has no comparable figures for Amazon, Alphabet or Meta, and nothing on whether the revenue was 'magnitudes higher' relative to capex. On this packet the claim stays unresolved.
